all solutions $(x, y)$ are integers. Try to find the value of $a$.

meta.gold_solution:
From equation (1), we get $y=(a+1) x$. Substituting into equation (2), we have
$$
(a+1) x^{2}-\left(a^{2}+1\right) x+2 a^{3}-2=0 \text {. }
$$

When $a=-1$, equation (3) can be simplified to $-2 x-4=0$.
Solving, we get $x=-2, y=0$, which meets the requirements.
When $a \neq-1$, we have
$$
x_{1}+x_{2}=\frac{a^{2}+1}{a+1}=a-1+\frac{2}{a+1} \text {. }
$$

For $x_{1} 、 x_{2}$ to be integers, $\frac{2}{a+1}$ must be an integer.
Thus, $a+1= \pm 1, \pm 2$, which means
$$
a=0,-2,-3,1 \text {. }
$$
(1) When $a=0$, equation (3) becomes $x^{2}-x-2=0$.

Solving, we get $x_{1}=2, x_{2}=-1$.
In this case, $y_{1}=2, y_{2}=-1$, which meets the requirements.
(2) When $a=-2$, equation (3) becomes $-x^{2}-5 x-18=0$, which has no real solutions.
(3) When $a=-3$, equation (3) becomes $-2 x^{2}-10 x-56=0$, which has no real solutions.
(4) When $a=1$, equation (3) becomes $2 x^{2}-2 x=0$, solving which gives $x_{1}=0, x_{2}=1$.
In this case, $y_{1}=0, y_{2}=2$, which meets the requirements.
In summary, $a$ can take the values $-1,0,1$.

question:
## Task A-3.1. (4 points)

Determine all $x \in[0,2 \pi]$ for which $3 \sin x$ and $\frac{4}{7} \cos (2 x)+\frac{5}{3} \sin x$ are integers.

meta.gold_solution:
## Solution.

Let $n=3 \sin x \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then $-3 \leqslant n \leqslant 3$, so $n \in\{-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3\}$. (1 point) The expression $\frac{4}{7} \cos (2 x)+\frac{5}{3} \sin x$ is then equal to:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{4}{7}\left(\cos ^{2} x-\sin ^{2} x\right)+\frac{5}{3} \sin x=\frac{4}{7}\left(1-2 \sin ^{2} x\right)+\frac{5}{3} \sin x \\
& =\frac{4}{7}\left(1-2 \cdot \frac{n^{2}}{9}\right)+\frac{5}{3} \cdot \frac{n}{3}=\frac{-8 n^{2}+35 n+36}{63}
\end{aligned}
$$

By substituting the numbers from the set $\{-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3\}$ into the last expression, we find that it is an integer only for $n=1$.

(1 point)

From this, we conclude that the conditions of the problem are satisfied by all real numbers $x$ for which $3 \sin x=1$, or $\sin x=\frac{1}{3}$. In the given interval $[0,2 \pi]$, we have two solutions: $x_{1}=\arcsin \frac{1}{3}$ and $x_{2}=\pi-\arcsin \frac{1}{3}$.

(1 point)

question:
## Task 6

Divide and justify the results using multiplication. 40 by $4 ; \quad 24$ by $3 ; \quad 40$ by 5

Dona Lígia has a square plot of land. She decides to divide it into five regions, consisting of four rectangles and one square as illustrated in the figure below:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_01_d18780f0fd52e0502cf8g-20.jpg?height=416&width=417&top_left_y=503&top_left_x=725)

$\mathrm{In}$ the figure above, we have that:

- The central square has an area of $64 \mathrm{~m}^{2}$;
- The longer sides of the four rectangles have the same length;
- The five regions have the same perimeter.

Determine the area of Dona Lígia's plot of land.

meta.gold_solution:
Solution

Since the area of the central square is equal to $64 \mathrm{~m}^{2}$, its side length is $8 \mathrm{~m}$. Since the perimeter of a square is four times the length of its side, we conclude that the perimeter of the central square is equal to $32 \mathrm{~m}$.

Since the five regions have the same perimeter, we conclude that the perimeter of each rectangle is also equal to $32 \mathrm{~m}$. Now observe the following figure:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_01_d18780f0fd52e0502cf8g-49.jpg?height=466&width=525&top_left_y=1857&top_left_x=868)

From this, we see that $M A + A N$ is equal to half the perimeter of rectangle MANS. Therefore,

$$
M A + A N = 16 \mathrm{~m}
$$

But the longer sides of the rectangles are equal, i.e., $M A = N B$. Thus, we can substitute $M A$ with $N B$ in equation (.4) to get $N B + A N = 16 \mathrm{~m}$. We conclude then that the side of the plot measures $N B + A N = 16 \mathrm{~m}$. Since the plot is square-shaped, the area of the plot is $(16 \mathrm{~m})^{2} = 256 \mathrm{~m}^{2}$.

question:
Example 8 Find the maximum value of $n$ such that there exists an arithmetic sequence $a_{1}, a_{2}, \cdots, a_{n}(n \geqslant 3)$ satisfying
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|a_{i}\right|=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|a_{i}+1\right|=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|a_{i}-2\right|=507 .
$$
(2005, China Southeast Mathematical Olympiad)

meta.gold_solution:
【Analysis】Let's assume $a_{i}=a-i d(d>0, i=1,2$, $\cdots, n)$. Then the given system of equations becomes
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}|a-i d|=507, \\
\sum_{i=1}^{n}|a+1-i d|=507, \\
\sum_{i=1}^{n}|a-2-i d|=507 .
\end{array}\right.
$$

Thus, the absolute value sum function $f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|x-i d|$ has three "equal value points":
$$
f(a-2)=f(a)=f(a+1)=507,
$$

which implies that $n=2 k\left(k \in \mathbf{Z}_{+}\right)$, and
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
a-2, a, a+1 \in[k d,(k+1) d], \\
f(k d)=507
\end{array}\right. \\
\Rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}
d \geqslant 3, \\
k^{2} d=507
\end{array}\right. \\
\Rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}
d \geqslant 3, \\
k^{2}=\frac{507}{d} \leqslant \frac{507}{3}=169
\end{array}\right. \\
\Rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}
d \geqslant 3, \\
k \leqslant 13 .
\end{array}\right.
\end{array}
$$

Therefore, $n \leqslant 26$, with equality holding when $d=3, k=13$.
Thus, $a-2=k d=39$, which means $a=41$. The corresponding arithmetic sequence is $\{41-3 k\}(k=1,2, \cdots, 26)$.
Hence, $n_{\max }=26$.
【Note】This example essentially involves the positioning and calculation of the minimum value of the absolute value sum function
$$
f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|x-i d|
$$

question:
There are two hourglasses - one for 7 minutes and one for 11 minutes. An egg needs to boil for 15 minutes. How can you measure this time using the available hourglasses?

#

meta.gold_solution:
With the help of two different hourglasses, you can measure not only the time equal to their "sum," but also the time equal to their "difference."

## Solution

"Start" both hourglasses simultaneously. When the 7-minute hourglass runs out, flip it and let it run for 4 more minutes until the 11-minute hourglass runs out. If you now flip the 7-minute hourglass again, it will run for exactly 4 more minutes, and in total, the hourglasses have been running for 15 minutes.

question:
1. Arun and Disha have some numbered discs to share out between them. They want to end up with one pile each, not necessarily of the same size, where Arun's pile contains exactly one disc numbered with a multiple of 2 and Disha's pile contains exactly one disc numbered with a multiple of 3 . For each case below, either count the number of ways of sharing the discs, or explain why it is impossible to share them in this way.
(a) They start with ten discs numbered from 1 to 10 .
(b) They start with twenty discs numbered from 1 to 20 .

meta.gold_solution:
SolUtion
(a) Consider the disc numbered 6. Assume for the moment that it is in Arun's pile. Then all the other discs numbered with a multiple of 2 must be in Disha's pile.
Disha's pile must also contain one of the two remaining discs numbered with a multiple of 3 (with the other in Arun's pile), so there are ${ }^{2} C_{1}=2$ ways to arrange the remaining discs numbered with a multiple of 3 .
Once the discs containing multiples of 3 have been allocated to a pile, there are three remaining discs (those numbered 1,5 and 7), each of which could go in either of the two piles, so there are $2^{3}=8$ ways this can be done.
So there are $2 \times 8=16$ ways of distributing the discs if the disc numbered 6 is in Arun's pile.
Now assume that the disc numbered 6 is in Disha's pile. Then all the other discs numbered with a multiple of 3 must be in Arun's pile.
Arun's pile must also contain one of the four remaining discs numbered with a multiple of 2 (with the other three all in Disha's pile), so there are ${ }^{4} C_{1}=4$ ways to arrange the remaining discs numbered with a multiple of 2 .
Once the discs containing multiples of 2 have been allocated to a pile, there are again three remaining discs ( 1,5 and 7 ), and as before there are 8 ways these can be allocated to the piles.
So there are $4 \times 8=32$ ways of distributing the discs if the disc numbered 6 is in Disha's pile.
Hence there are $16+32=48$ ways they can share the discs out.
(b) Consider the three discs numbered 6,12 and 18, which are multiples of both 2 and 3 . Since there are three of them, when the discs are shared out, one of Arun's and Disha's pile must contain (at least) two of them. But that is against the rules for how Arun and Disha want to share the discs out, so it is impossible to share them out.

question:
Tokaeva I.

Let $F_{1}, F_{2}, F_{3}, \ldots$ be a sequence of convex quadrilaterals, where $F_{k+1}$ (for $k=1,2,3, \ldots$) is obtained by cutting $F_{k}$ along a diagonal, flipping one of the parts, and gluing it back along the cut line to the other part. What is the maximum number of different quadrilaterals that this sequence can contain? (Quadrilaterals are considered different if they cannot be made to coincide by a movement.)

meta.gold_solution:
Let $ABCD$ be the original quadrilateral $F_{1}$. We can assume that each time the half of the quadrilateral containing side $CD$ is flipped, while side $AB$ remains stationary. In this process, the sum of angle $A$ and the opposite angle does not change. Additionally, the set of side lengths does not change. However, the three lengths (sides other than $AB$) can be ordered in only six ways.

We will prove that if two resulting quadrilaterals $ABKL$ and $ABMN$ have the same ordered side lengths ($BK = BM$, $KL = MN$, $LA = NA$), then the quadrilaterals are equal. It is sufficient to prove the equality of the diagonals $AK$ and $AM$. Assuming, for example, that $AK > AM$, we get $\angle ABK > \angle ABM$, $\angle ALK > \angle ANM$, which contradicts the equality of the sums $\angle ABK + \angle ALK$ and $\angle ABM + \angle ANM$.

Six different quadrilaterals will result from any quadrilateral where all sides are different, the sums of opposite angles are also different, and the quadrilateral remains convex and does not degenerate into a triangle during transformations. Only quadrilaterals with the reverse order of sides might be suspected of being equal, but they are not equal either, since flipping one of them will not align the sums of opposite angles. The highlighted condition is satisfied, for example, for quadrilaterals whose area is greater than half the product of the two longest sides: this inequality is clearly not true for non-convex and degenerate quadrilaterals. A specific example: a right trapezoid with bases 3 and 6 and height 4.

## Answer

6 quadrilaterals.

question:
Let $A$ and $B$ be two sets of non-negative integers, define $A+B$ as the set of the values obtained when we sum any (one) element of the set $A$ with any (one) element of the set $B$. For instance, if $A=\{2,3\}$ and $B=\{0,1,2,5\}$ so $A+B=\{2,3,4,5,7,8\}$.
Determine the least integer $k$ such that there is a pair of sets $A$ and $B$ of non-negative integers with $k$ and $2k$ elements, respectively, and
$A+B=\{0,1,2,\dots, 2019,2020\}$

meta.gold_solution:
1. We need to determine the least integer \( k \) such that there exist sets \( A \) and \( B \) with \( k \) and \( 2k \) elements, respectively, and \( A + B = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 2019, 2020\} \).

2. The set \( A + B \) contains all integers from 0 to 2020, which means \( |A + B| = 2021 \).

3. The maximum number of distinct sums \( |A + B| \) occurs when all sums of elements from \( A \) and \( B \) are distinct. This would be the case if \( A \) and \( B \) are chosen such that each sum \( a + b \) (where \( a \in A \) and \( b \in B \)) is unique.

4. If \( A \) has \( k \) elements and \( B \) has \( 2k \) elements, the number of possible sums is \( k \times 2k = 2k^2 \).

5. We need \( 2k^2 \geq 2021 \) to cover all integers from 0 to 2020. Solving for \( k \):
   \[
   2k^2 \geq 2021
   \]
   \[
   k^2 \geq \frac{2021}{2}
   \]
   \[
   k^2 \geq 1010.5
   \]
   \[
   k \geq \sqrt{1010.5}
   \]
   \[
   k \geq 31.78
   \]
   Since \( k \) must be an integer, we round up to the nearest whole number:
   \[
   k \geq 32
   \]

6. To verify, we can construct sets \( A \) and \( B \) with \( k = 32 \):
   \[
   A = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 31\}
   \]
   \[
   B = \{0, 32, 64, \ldots, 1984, 1989\}
   \]
   The set \( A + B \) will contain all integers from 0 to 2020 because each element in \( A \) can be paired with each element in \( B \) to produce a unique sum.

Conclusion:
The least integer \( k \) such that there exist sets \( A \) and \( B \) with \( k \) and \( 2k \) elements, respectively, and \( A + B = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 2019, 2020\} \) is \( \boxed{32} \).

question:
Find the minimum value of $k$ such that there exists two sequence ${a_i},{b_i}$ for $i=1,2,\cdots ,k$ that satisfies the following conditions.

(i) For all $i=1,2,\cdots ,k,$ $a_i,b_i$ is the element of $S=\{1996^n|n=0,1,2,\cdots\}.$
(ii) For all $i=1,2,\cdots, k, a_i\ne b_i.$
(iii) For all $i=1,2,\cdots, k, a_i\le a_{i+1}$ and $b_i\le b_{i+1}.$
(iv) $\sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i=\sum_{i=1}^{k} b_i.$

meta.gold_solution:
1. **Define the Set \( S \)**:
   The set \( S \) is given by \( S = \{1996^n \mid n = 0, 1, 2, \cdots\} \). This means \( S \) contains powers of 1996, i.e., \( S = \{1, 1996, 1996^2, 1996^3, \cdots\} \).

2. **Conditions to Satisfy**:
   - \( a_i, b_i \in S \) for all \( i = 1, 2, \cdots, k \).
   - \( a_i \neq b_i \) for all \( i = 1, 2, \cdots, k \).
   - \( a_i \leq a_{i+1} \) and \( b_i \leq b_{i+1} \) for all \( i = 1, 2, \cdots, k-1 \).
   - \( \sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i = \sum_{i=1}^{k} b_i \).

3. **Initial Assumption**:
   Let \( a_1 = 1996^x \) and \( b_1 = 1996^y \). Without loss of generality, assume \( x > y \).

4. **Modulo Condition**:
   Since \( \sum a_i \equiv 0 \pmod{1996^{y+1}} \), it follows that \( \sum b_i \equiv 0 \pmod{1996^{y+1}} \). This implies that there must be at least 1996 terms of \( 1996^y \) in the sequence \( b_i \).

5. **Minimum \( k \) Analysis**:
   - If \( k = 1996 \), then \( \sum b_i = 1996^{y+1} \leq a_1 < \sum a_i \). This inequality shows that \( k = 1996 \) is not sufficient.
   - Therefore, \( k \) must be greater than 1996.

6. **Constructing Sequences for \( k = 1997 \)**:
   - Let \( a_1 = 1996 \) and \( a_i = 1996^2 \) for \( i = 2, 3, \cdots, 1997 \).
   - Let \( b_j = 1 \) for \( j = 1, 2, \cdots, 1996 \) and \( b_{1997} = 1996^3 \).

7. **Verification**:
   - Calculate \( \sum_{i=1}^{1997} a_i \):
     \[
     \sum_{i=1}^{1997} a_i = 1996 + 1996^2 \times 1996 = 1996 + 1996^3
     \]
   - Calculate \( \sum_{i=1}^{1997} b_i \):
     \[
     \sum_{i=1}^{1997} b_i = 1996 \times 1 + 1996^3 = 1996 + 1996^3
     \]
   - Both sums are equal, satisfying the condition \( \sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i = \sum_{i=1}^{k} b_i \).

Thus, the minimum value of \( k \) that satisfies all the conditions is \( 1997 \).

The final answer is \( \boxed{1997} \).

question: BEL   Let $A B C$ be a triangle with $A B=A C$. The angle bisectors of $A$ and $B$ meet the sides $B C$ and $A C$ in $D$ and $E$, respectively. Let $K$ be the incenter of triangle $A D C$. Suppose that $\angle B E K=45^{\circ}$. Find all possible values of $\angle B A C$.

meta.gold_solution: Answer: $\angle B A C=60^{\circ}$ or $\angle B A C=90^{\circ}$ are possible values and the only possible values. Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $A B C$, then $K$ lies on the line $C I$. Let $F$ be the point, where the incircle of triangle $A B C$ touches the side $A C$; then the segments $I F$ and $I D$ have the same length and are perpendicular to $A C$ and $B C$, respectively. ![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_11_18_b191c9407e8cb3d672cbg-49.jpg?height=549&width=615&top_left_y=1025&top_left_x=252)  Figure 1 ![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_11_18_b191c9407e8cb3d672cbg-49.jpg?height=510&width=901&top_left_y=1067&top_left_x=906)  Figure 2  Let $P, Q$ and $R$ be the points where the incircle of triangle $A D C$ touches the sides $A D, D C$ and $C A$, respectively. Since $K$ and $I$ lie on the angle bisector of $\angle A C D$, the segments $I D$ and $I F$ are symmetric with respect to the line $I C$. Hence there is a point $S$ on $I F$ where the incircle of triangle $A D C$ touches the segment $I F$. Then segments $K P, K Q, K R$ and $K S$ all have the same length and are perpendicular to $A D, D C, C A$ and $I F$, respectively. So - regardless of the value of $\angle B E K$ - the quadrilateral $K R F S$ is a square and $\angle S F K=\angle K F C=45^{\circ}$. Consider the case $\angle B A C=60^{\circ}$ (see Figure 1). Then triangle $A B C$ is equilateral. Furthermore we have $F=E$, hence $\angle B E K=\angle I F K=\angle S E K=45^{\circ}$. So $60^{\circ}$ is a possible value for $\angle B A C$. Now consider the case $\angle B A C=90^{\circ}$ (see Figure 2). Then $\angle C B A=\angle A C B=45^{\circ}$. Furthermore, $\angle K I E=\frac{1}{2} \angle C B A+\frac{1}{2} \angle A C B=45^{\circ}, \angle A E B=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-22.5^{\circ}=67.5^{\circ}$ and $\angle E I A=\angle B I D=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-22.5^{\circ}=67.5^{\circ}$. Hence triangle $I E A$ is isosceles and a reflection of the bisector of $\angle I A E$ takes $I$ to $E$ and $K$ to itself. So triangle $I K E$ is symmetric with respect to this axis, i.e. $\angle K I E=\angle I E K=\angle B E K=45^{\circ}$. So $90^{\circ}$ is a possible value for $\angle B A C$, too. If, on the other hand, $\angle B E K=45^{\circ}$ then $\angle B E K=\angle I E K=\angle I F K=45^{\circ}$. Then  - either $F=E$, which makes the angle bisector $B I$ be an altitude, i.e., which makes triangle $A B C$ isosceles with base $A C$ and hence equilateral and so $\angle B A C=60^{\circ}$, - or $E$ lies between $F$ and $C$, which makes the points $K, E, F$ and $I$ concyclic, so $45^{\circ}=$ $\angle K F C=\angle K F E=\angle K I E=\angle C B I+\angle I C B=2 \cdot \angle I C B=90^{\circ}-\frac{1}{2} \angle B A C$, and so $\angle B A C=90^{\circ}$, - or $F$ lies between $E$ and $C$, then again, $K, E, F$ and $I$ are concyclic, so $45^{\circ}=\angle K F C=$ $180^{\circ}-\angle K F E=\angle K I E$, which yields the same result $\angle B A C=90^{\circ}$. (However, for $\angle B A C=90^{\circ} E$ lies, in fact, between $F$ and $C$, see Figure 2. So this case does not occur.) This proves $90^{\circ}$ and $60^{\circ}$ to be the only possible values for $\angle B A C$.

question:
Boris has special digital watches. They are accurate, but instead of hours and minutes, they show two other numbers: the first is the sum of the digits that would normally be on the display, and the second is the sum of the hours and minutes (for example, at 7:30, they show 10:37).

What time could it be when Boris's watches show 6:15? Determine all possibilities.

(M. Dillingerová)

Hint. Can some digits in the normal time representation be ruled out in advance?

meta.gold_solution:
The sum of the digits showing the actual time is 6, so none of the digits is greater than 6. The sum of the numbers showing the actual hours and minutes is 15. Using the digits from 0 to 6, 15 can be expressed as the sum of two numbers in the following ways:

$$
0+15, \quad 1+14, \quad 2+13, \quad 3+12, \quad 4+11, \quad 5+10
$$

When Boris's clock shows $6:15$, it could be $0:15, 1:14, 2:13, 3:12, 4:11, 5:10, 10:05$, 11:04, 12:03, 13:02, 14:01, or 15:00.

Note. Part of the task is also to describe the process leading to the correct answer. The times listed without a proper explanation cannot be rated at the highest level.

question: Example 3 A password lock's password setting involves assigning one of the two numbers, 0 or 1, to each vertex of a regular $n$-sided polygon $A_{1} A_{2} \cdots A_{n}$, and coloring each vertex either red or blue, such that for any two adjacent vertices, at least one of the number or color is the same. How many different password settings are there for this type of password lock?

meta.gold_solution:
Let $S_{n}$ be the desired result, and let $a_{n}, b_{n}, c_{n}$ represent the number of ways to set the password when $A_{n}=A_{1}$, $A_{n} \neq A_{1}$, and $A_{n} \# A_{1}$, respectively.
Then $S_{n}=a_{n}+b_{n}$.
It is easy to see that $\left(a_{1}, b_{1}, c_{1}\right)=(4,0,0)$,
$\left(a_{2}, b_{2}, c_{2}\right)=(4,8,4)$,
$\left(a_{3}, b_{3}, c_{3}\right)=(12,16,8)$.
When $n \geqslant 4$, we consider three cases.
(1) $A_{n}=A_{1}$, then $A_{n}$ and $A_{1}$ are effectively one point, so $a_{n}=a_{n-1}+b_{n-1}$.
(2) $A_{n} \neq A_{1}$, consider $A_{n-1}$.
(i) $A_{n-1}=A_{1}$, then there are $a_{n-1}$ ways from $A_{1}$ to $A_{n-1}$, and $A_{n}$ has 2 ways, so there are $2 a_{n-1}$ ways.
(ii) $A_{n-1} \neq A_{1}$, then $A_{n-1}=A_{n}$, and considering $A_{n-1}$ and $A_{n}$ as one point, there are $b_{n-1}$ ways.
(iii) $A_{n-1} \# A_{1}$, consider $A_{n-2}$.
If $A_{n-2}=A_{1} \# A_{n-1}$, it is a contradiction.
If $A_{n-2} \neq A_{1}$, then there are $b_{n-2}$ ways from $A_{1}$ to $A_{n-2}$, and $A_{n-1}$ and $A_{n}$ have 1 and 2 ways respectively, so there are $2 b_{n-2}$ ways; $\square$

If $A_{n-2} \# A_{1}$, then $A_{n-2}=A_{n-1}$, and considering $A_{n-2}$ and $A_{n-1}$ as one point, there are $2 c_{n-2}$ ways.
In summary, $b_{n}=2 a_{n-1}+b_{n-1}+2 b_{n-2}+2 c_{n-2}$.
(3) $A_{n} \# A_{1}$, similarly we have
$$
c_{n}=b_{n-1}+c_{n-1} \text {. }
$$

Combining equations (1) and (4), we get
$$
S_{n}=3^{n}+(-1)^{n}+2
$$

question: A square-based pyramid has all edges 2 units long. We attach a pyramid to one of the side faces of the pyramid, where the side edges of the new pyramid are of equal length. The total length of the edges of the resulting solid is 18 units. What is the volume of the solid?

meta.gold_solution:
The base of the pyramid $A B C D E$ is a square, and every edge is 2 units long, so the side faces are equilateral triangles. The edges of the added pyramid $B C E F$ are equal, making $B C E F$ a regular pyramid. The side edges of this pyramid are longer than the distance from the center of the equilateral triangle $B C E$ to its vertices, so the total length of the side edges is at least $3 \cdot \frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{3}=2 \sqrt{3}>2$. Therefore, the total length of the edges of the resulting solid can only be 18 if some edges of the original pyramid coincide with the faces of the new solid. The vertex $F$ is located perpendicularly above the centroid of the triangle $E B C$, so $F$ cannot lie in the plane of $A B C D$. If $F$ lies in the plane of $A B E$, then, since the perpendicular bisector plane of the segment $B C$ is a symmetry plane for both the original pyramid and the pyramid $B C E F$, $F$ must also lie in the plane of $C D E$. Therefore, the edges $B E$ and $C E$ of the original pyramid must coincide with the faces of the new solid. The total length of the edges of the new solid will be exactly 18 units if $B F=C F=E F=2$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_17e75dc0d6cc397fdf3cg-1.jpg?height=583&width=775&top_left_y=584&top_left_x=664)

According to this, the resulting solid consists of a square pyramid and a regular tetrahedron. The height of the square pyramid can be easily determined using the Pythagorean theorem in the triangle $A C E$: $\sqrt{2}$, so its volume is $\frac{4 \sqrt{2}}{3}$. The volume of the regular tetrahedron with an edge length of 2 units is $\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3}$. Therefore, the volume of the resulting solid is $2 \sqrt{2}$.

question:
a) Calculate the sum of the squares of the roots of the equation $(x+2)(x-1)(x-3)=2$.

b) Prove that the following equation cannot have all real roots:

$$
x^{10}-2 x^{9}+5 x^{8}+a x^{7}-b x^{6}+c x^{5}+d x^{4}+e x^{3}+f x^{2}+g x+h=0 .
$$

meta.gold_solution:
a) By reducing the equation to 0 and breaking it into terms, we can bring it to the form

$$
x^{3}-2 x^{2}-5 x+4=0
$$

If the roots of the equation are $\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \alpha_{3}$, then the left side must match term by term with the expanded form of

$$
\left(x-\alpha_{1}\right)\left(x-\alpha_{2}\right)\left(x-\alpha_{3}\right)
$$

because the highest degree term of both polynomials is $x^{3}$. Thus,

$$
\begin{gathered}
x^{3}-2 x^{2}-5 x+4-\left(x-\alpha_{1}\right)\left(x-\alpha_{2}\right)\left(x-\alpha_{3}\right)=\left(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{3}-2\right) x^{2}- \\
-\left(\alpha_{1} \alpha_{2}+\alpha_{1} \alpha_{3}+\alpha_{2} \alpha_{3}+5\right)+\left(\alpha_{1} \alpha_{2} \alpha_{3}+4\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

This difference, on the one hand, takes the value 0 at $\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \alpha_{3}$, and on the other hand, can be at most a quadratic polynomial, and thus can vanish at most two places if not all the coefficients on the right side are 0. Therefore,

$$
\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{3}=2, \quad \alpha_{1} \alpha_{2}+\alpha_{1} \alpha_{3}+\alpha_{2} \alpha_{3}=-5, \quad \alpha_{1} \alpha_{2} \alpha_{3}=-4
$$

Using the first two, we get

$$
\alpha_{1}^{2}+\alpha_{2}^{2}+\alpha_{3}^{2}=\left(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{3}\right)^{2}-2\left(\alpha_{1} \alpha_{2}+\alpha_{1} \alpha_{3}+\alpha_{2} \alpha_{3}\right)=2^{2}-2(-5)=14
$$

b) The facts used here are not limited to cubic equations. Generally, if a polynomial of degree $n$

$$
f(x)=a_{0} x^{n}+a_{1} x^{n-1}+a_{2} x^{n-2}+\ldots+a_{n-1} x+a_{n}
$$

vanishes at $\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \ldots, \alpha_{n}$, then it can be rearranged as

$$
a_{0}\left(x-\alpha_{1}\right)\left(x-\alpha_{2}\right) \ldots\left(x-\alpha_{n}\right)
$$

and the following relationships hold between the roots and coefficients:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{1} & =-a_{0}\left(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\ldots+\alpha_{n}\right) \\
a_{2} & =a_{0}\left(\alpha_{1} \alpha_{2}+\alpha_{1} \alpha_{3}+\ldots \alpha_{n-1} \alpha_{n}\right) \\
a_{3} & =-a_{0}\left(\alpha_{1} \alpha_{2} \alpha_{3}+\alpha_{1} \alpha_{2} \alpha_{4}+\ldots+\alpha_{n-2} \alpha_{n-1} \alpha_{n}\right), \ldots \\
a_{n} & =(-1)^{n} a_{0} \alpha_{1} \alpha_{2} \ldots \alpha_{n}
\end{aligned}
$$

Generally, $a_{k}$ can be obtained by selecting $k$ of the $\alpha$'s in every possible way, multiplying them, and then multiplying the sum of the products by $a_{0}$ or $(-a_{0})$ depending on whether $k$ is even or odd.

If, specifically, the roots of equation (1) are $\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}, \ldots, \beta_{10}$, to calculate their sum of squares, it is sufficient to know the coefficients of the 9th and 8th degree terms:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\ldots+\beta_{10}=-2 \\
\beta_{1} \beta_{2}+\ldots+\beta_{1} \beta_{10}+\beta_{2} \beta_{3}+\ldots+\beta_{9} \beta_{10}=5
\end{gathered}
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta_{1}^{2} \beta_{2}^{2}+\ldots+\beta_{10}^{2} & =\left(\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\ldots+\beta_{10}\right)^{2}-2\left(\beta_{1} \beta_{2}+\beta_{1} \beta_{3}+\ldots+\right. \\
& \left.+\beta_{9} \beta_{10}\right)=(-2)^{2}-2 \cdot 5=-6
\end{aligned}
$$

This is impossible in the realm of real numbers, so it cannot be that equation (1) has 10 real roots, which is what we needed to prove. Horányi Sándor (Budapest, Móricz Zs. g. IV. o. t.)

Note. We assumed that our equations have as many roots as their degree. In the case of (a), this can be seen from the fact that the left side of the reduced equation takes the values $-2, 4, -6, 16$ at $-2, 0, 2, 4$ respectively. These values have alternating signs, so between each pair of adjacent points, it takes the value 0.

Part (b) can be considered an indirect proof: If there were 10 (real) roots, their sum of squares would have to be positive, which is impossible. If we rely on the knowledge of complex numbers as well, it is known that every (at least first-degree) polynomial has a root in the complex numbers. From this, it follows - using [3], that if a polynomial vanishes at $\alpha$, the factor $x-\alpha$ can be factored out - that a polynomial of degree $n$ has $n$ roots in the complex numbers, counting multiplicities. Thus, equation (1) also has 10 roots in the complex numbers, but they cannot all be real because their sum of squares is negative. (It is possible that none of them are real.)[^0]

[^0]:    ${ }^{1}$ See, for example, János Surányi: Polynomial Identity, K. M. L. 23 (1961/11.), pp. 103-105.

    ${ }^{2}$ We arrive at these by introducing a new number $i$, the imaginary unit, whose square is -1. Its real multiples are the imaginary numbers, and the sum of a real and an imaginary number gives the complex numbers. In the realm of complex numbers, the basic operations can be defined such that the usual operational rules remain valid for them. In the realm of complex numbers, every (at least first-degree) polynomial has a root. See, for example, Tamás Varga: Comprehensive Mathematics for Maturity, Tankönyvkiadó, Budapest, 1961, 11th edition, pp. 55-57; and Richárd Rieger: Complex Numbers, Középiskolai Szakköri Füzetek, Tankönyvkiadó, Budapest, 1954.

    ${ }^{3}$ See, for example, the article cited in the first footnote.

question: 11. (20 points) In the Cartesian coordinate system, points $A$, $B$, and $C$ lie on the hyperbola $x y=1$, satisfying that $\triangle ABC$ is an isosceles right triangle. Find the minimum value of the area of $\triangle ABC$.

meta.gold_solution:
11. As shown in Figure 2, let's assume the vertices $A, B, C$ of the isosceles right triangle $\triangle ABC$ are arranged counterclockwise, with $A$ being the right-angle vertex.
Let $\overrightarrow{A B}=(s, t)$.
Then $\overrightarrow{A C}=(-t, s)$,

and the area of $\triangle ABC$ is
$$
\begin{array}{l}
S_{\triangle A B C}=\frac{1}{2}|\overrightarrow{A B}|^{2} \\
=\frac{s^{2}+t^{2}}{2} .
\end{array}
$$

Note that, point $A$ lies on the hyperbola $x y=1$.
Let $A\left(a, \frac{1}{a}\right)$. Then
$$
B\left(a+s, \frac{1}{a}+t\right), C\left(a-t, \frac{1}{a}+s\right) \text {. }
$$

Since points $B$ and $C$ lie on the hyperbola $x y=1$, we have
$$
(a+s)\left(\frac{1}{a}+t\right)=(a-t)\left(\frac{1}{a}+s\right)=1 \text {, }
$$

which is equivalent to
$$
\begin{array}{c}
\frac{s}{a}+a t=-s t, \\
-\frac{t}{a}+a s=s t .
\end{array}
$$
Adding (1) and (2) gives
$\frac{s-t}{a}+a(t+s)=0$
$\Rightarrow a^{2}=\frac{t-s}{t+s}$.
Multiplying (1) and (2) and using equation (3) gives
$$
\begin{array}{l}
-s^{2} t^{2}=\left(\frac{s}{a}+a t\right)\left(-\frac{t}{a}+a s\right) \\
=\left(a^{2}-\frac{1}{a^{2}}\right) s t+s^{2}-t^{2} \\
=\left(\frac{t-s}{t+s}-\frac{t+s}{t-s}\right) s t+s^{2}-t^{2} \\
=\frac{4 s t}{s^{2}-t^{2}} \cdot s t+s^{2}-t^{2}=\frac{\left(s^{2}+t^{2}\right)^{2}}{s^{2}-t^{2}} .
\end{array}
$$

Thus, by the AM-GM inequality, we have
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\left(s^{2}+t^{2}\right)^{4}=\left(-s^{2} t^{2}\left(s^{2}-t^{2}\right)\right)^{2} \\
=\frac{1}{4} \cdot 2 s^{2} t^{2} \cdot 2 s^{2} t^{2}\left(s^{2}-t^{2}\right)^{2} \\
\leqslant \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{2 s^{2} t^{2}+2 s^{2} t^{2}+\left(s^{2}-t^{2}\right)^{2}}{3}\right)^{3} \\
=\frac{\left(s^{2}+t^{2}\right)^{6}}{108} \\
\Rightarrow s^{2}+t^{2} \geqslant \sqrt{108}=6 \sqrt{3} .
\end{array}
$$

Now, let's find a set of real numbers $(s, t, a)$ that satisfy the conditions, such that $s^{2}+t^{2}=6 \sqrt{3}$ (and thus by $s, t, a$ we can determine a $\triangle ABC$ that satisfies the conditions, with $S_{\triangle A B C}=\frac{s^{2}+t^{2}}{2}=3 \sqrt{3}$).
Considering the equality condition of equation (4), we have
$$
2 s^{2} t^{2}=\left(s^{2}-t^{2}\right)^{2} \Rightarrow \frac{s^{2}}{t^{2}}=2 \pm \sqrt{3} \text {. }
$$

Assuming $0<s<t$, and combining with $s^{2}+t^{2}=6 \sqrt{3}$, we get $s=\sqrt{3(\sqrt{3}-1)}, t=\sqrt{3(\sqrt{3}+1)}$.
From equation (1), we know $a<0$. Hence, from equation (3), we get
$a=-\sqrt{\frac{t-s}{t+s}}\left(t=s \sqrt{\frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{\sqrt{3}-1}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{\sqrt{2}} s\right)$.
Therefore, $a=-\sqrt{\frac{\sqrt{3}+1-\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}+1+\sqrt{2}}}$.
In summary, the minimum area of $\triangle ABC$ is $3 \sqrt{3}$.

2. (1) When $AB$ is not a perpendicular chord, let $l_{AB}: y=kx+b$. Combining with $S$ we get
$\left(1-4k^{2}\right)x^{2}-8kbx-4b^{2}-8=0$.
From $AB$ intersecting the hyperbola at two points, we know
$k \neq \pm \frac{1}{2}$.
Let $A\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right), B\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)$.
By Vieta's formulas, we get $x_{1} \star x_{2}=\frac{8kb}{1-4k^{2}}$.
Let the midpoint of $AB$ be $C\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right)$. Then
$x_{0}=\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}}{2}=\frac{4kb}{1-4k^{2}}$,
$y_{0}=\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}}{2}=\frac{kx_{1}+b+kx_{2}+b}{2}=\frac{b}{1-4k^{2}}$.
Also, the distance from point $C$ to $l_{1}: x-2y=0$ is 1, so $\frac{\left|x_{0}-2y_{0}\right|}{\sqrt{5}}=1$, which means $\left|\frac{b}{1+2k}\right|=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$.
It is easy to find that the intersection point of $l_{2}: x+2y=0$ and $AB$ is $D\left(\frac{-2b}{2k+1}, \frac{b}{2k+1}\right)$.
Thus, $|OD|=\sqrt{\left(\frac{-2b}{2k+1}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{b}{2k+1}\right)^{2}}$ $=\sqrt{5}\left|\frac{b}{2k+1}\right|=\frac{5}{2}$.
When $AB \perp x$-axis, it is easy to get $|OD|=\frac{5}{2}$.
Therefore, $|OD|=\frac{5}{2}$.
(2) From (1), when $AB$ is not a perpendicular chord,
$x_{1}+x_{2}=\frac{8kb}{1-4k^{2}}, x_{1}x_{2}=\frac{-4\left(b^{2}+2\right)}{1-4k^{2}}$.
Thus, $|AB|^{2}=\left(1+k^{2}\right)\left(x_{1}-x_{2}\right)^{2}$
$=\left(1+k^{2}\right)\left[\left(x_{1}+x_{2}\right)^{2}-4x_{1}x_{2}\right]$.
Since $AB=4$, rearranging gives $b^{2}=\frac{\left(6k^{2}+1\right)\left(4k^{2}-1\right)}{1+k^{2}}$.
Thus, it is easy to see that $k^{2}>\frac{1}{4}$.
Also, $AB$ intersects $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ at points $P$ and $D$, and it is easy to calculate $P\left(\frac{2b}{1-2k}, \frac{b}{1-2k}\right)$ and $D\left(\frac{-2b}{2k+1}, \frac{b}{2k+1}\right)$.
Thus, $|PD|=\frac{4|b|\sqrt{1+k^{2}}}{4k^{2}-1}$.
The distance from point $O$ to $PD$ is $\frac{|b|}{\sqrt{1+k^{2}}}$.
Therefore, $S_{\triangle POD}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{|b|}{\sqrt{1+k^{2}}} \cdot \frac{4|b|\sqrt{1+k^{2}}}{4k^{2}-1}$ $=\frac{2b^{2}}{4k^{2}-1}=\frac{2\left(6k^{2}+1\right)}{1+k^{2}}$.
Since $k^{2}>\frac{1}{4}$, we know $S_{\triangle POD}>4, S_{\triangle POD}<12$.
When $AB \perp x$-axis, $S_{\triangle POD}=12$.
Thus, the range of $S_{\triangle POD}$ is $(4,12]$.

question: 42nd Putnam 1981 Problem A6 A, B, C are lattice points in the plane. The triangle ABC contains exactly one lattice point, X, in its interior. The line AX meets BC at E. What is the largest possible value of AX/XE? Solution

meta.gold_solution: : 5. Take A = (2, 4), B = (0, 0), C = (2, 1). This contains a single lattice point X (1, 1). B is a distance 2 from the line AC, and AC = 3, so ABC has area 3. B is a distance 1 from the line CX, and CX = 1, so XBC has area 1/2. So A is 6x the distance of X from BC. Hence AX = 5 XE. So the value 5 can certainly be achieved. Let L, M, N be the midpoints of BC, CA, AB. Let B have the coordinates (b 1 , b 2 ) and similarly for the other points. Take B' to be such that X is the midpoint of BB'. Then it is also a lattice point, since its coordinates are (2x 1 - b 1 , 2x 2 - b 2 ). So it cannot lie in the interior of the triangle ABC (since X is the only such lattice point). So X cannot lie in the interior of the triangle BNL (which has dimensions half that of BAC and is similar to it). Similarly, X cannot lie in the interior of CLM. Now consider the point L' on the ray LX such that LL' = 3LX. It is also a lattice point, since its coordinates are (3x 1 - (b 1 + c 1 ), 3x 2 - (b 2 + c 2 ) ). So it cannot lie in the interior of ABC. A fortiori, it cannot lie in the interior of LMN. Take M' on LM such that LM' = 1/3 LM, and N' on LN such that LN' = 1/3 LN. Then LM'N' is similar to LMN and 1/3 the dimensions. So X cannot lie inside LM'N' (otherwise L' would lie within LMN). It follows that X must lie above the extended line M'N' (which is parallel to BC). But the distance of this line above BC is 1/6 the distance of A above BC. So if the line AX cuts it at F (and BC at E), then AF/FE = 5. Hence AX/XE ≤ 5. 42nd Putnam 1981 © John Scholes jscholes@kalva.demon.co.uk 16 Jan 2001

7. The perimeter of a parallelogram is $30 \mathrm{~cm}$. The sum of the areas of the squares constructed on two adjacent sides is $113 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$. What are the lengths of those sides?

question: Example 9 In $\triangle A B C$, $O$ is the intersection of $A A^{\prime}$ and $B B^{\prime}$, $A^{\prime}$ is on $B C$, $B^{\prime}$ is on $A C$, and $S_{\triangle A O R^{\prime}}=3, S_{\triangle O A B}=2, S_{\triangle O A^{\prime} B}=1$. Find $S_{\triangle C A^{\prime} B^{\prime}}$.

meta.gold_solution:

S_{\triangle O A^{\prime} B}=\frac{A^{\prime} B}{B C} \cdot S_{\triangle O B C}=\frac{\lambda_{3}}{\lambda_{2}+\lambda_{3}} \cdot \lambda_{1}=1

$$

From the above, we get
$$
\lambda_{1}=S_{\triangle O B C}=10, \lambda_{2}=S_{\triangle O A C}=18
$$

Thus,

question: 13th APMO 2001 Problem 5 What is the largest n for which we can find n + 4 points in the plane, A, B, C, D, X 1 , ... , X n , so that AB is not equal to CD, but for each i the two triangles ABX i and CDX i are congruent?

meta.gold_solution: 4 Solution Many thanks to Allen Zhang for completing the proof Assume AB = a, CD = b with a > b. If ABX and CDX are congruent, then either AX or BX = CD = b, so X lies either on the circle S A center A radius b, or on the circle S B center B radius b. Similarly, CX or DX = AB = a, so X lies either on the circle S C center C radius a, or on the circle S D center D radius a. Thus we have four pairs of circles, (S A , S C ), (S A , S D ), (S B , S C ), (S B , S D ) each with at most 2 points of intersection. X must be one of these 8 points. However, we show that if two points of intersection of (S A , S C ) are included, then no points of (S B , S D ) can be included. The same applies to each pair of circles, so at most 4 points X are possible. Finally, we will give an example of n = 4, showing that the maximum of 4 is achieved. So suppose (S A , S C ) intersect at X and Y. We must have BX = DX and BY = DY, so X and Y both lie on the perpendicular bisector of BD. In other words, XY is the perpendicular bisector of BD, so D is the reflection of B in the line XY. There is no loss of generality in taking B (and D) to be on the same side of AC as X. Let A' be the reflection of A in the line XY. Since B lies on the circle center A radius a, D must lie on the circle center A' radius A. Thus the triangles A'XC and CDA' are congruent. (Note that A and C can be on the same side of XY or opposite sides.) Hence D is the same height above AC as X, so DX is perpendicular to XY. Hence X is the midpoint of BD. Also ∠A'CD = ∠CA'X = 180 o - ∠CAX, so AX and CD are parallel. They are also equal, so ACDX is a parallelogram and hence AC = DX = BD/2. In the second configuration above, both A and C are on the same side of XY as D, so the midpoint M of AC lies on the same side of XY as D. In the first configuration, since AX = b  b, so it must lie on the same side of XY as B. Contradiction. So there are no solutions for the configuration (S B , S D ), as required. That completes the proof that n ≤ 4. For an example with n = 4, take a regular hexagon ACDBX 3 X 2 . Extend the side X 2 X 3 to X 1 X 4 , with X 1 , X 2 , X 3 , X 4 equally spaced in that order, so that X 1 AX 2 and X 3 BX 4 are equilateral. Then ABX 1 and CX 1 D are congruent, ABX 2 and DX 2 C are congruent, ABX 3 and X 3 CD are congruent, and ABX 4 and X 4 DC are congruent. 13th APMO 2001 © John Scholes jscholes@kalva.demon.co.uk 8 February 2004 Last corrected/updated 8 Feb 04

question: 3. In an isosceles triangle $ABC$, the angle at the base is $\arcsin \frac{2}{3}$. A circle with its center at the midpoint of the base $BC$ intersects the line $AC$ at points $K$ and $L$, and the line $AB$ at points $M$ and $N$, such that segments $KM$ and $LN$ intersect. Find its radius if the radius of the circle passing through points $A, L$, and $N$ is 2.

meta.gold_solution:
# Problem 3.

Answer: $\frac{4 \sqrt{5}}{3}$.

Solution. Let point $O$ be the midpoint of the base $B C$. Without loss of generality, we assume that points $L$ and $M$ are closer to vertex $A$ than points $K$ and $N$ respectively. Due to symmetry with respect to the line $A O$, segment $M L$ is parallel to the base $B C$ and $\angle A M L=\angle A L M=\angle A B C=\arcsin \frac{2}{3}$. From the Law of Sines for $\triangle A L N$, we have: $L N=4 \sin \angle A=4 \sin \left(\pi-2 \arcsin \frac{2}{3}\right)=8 \cdot \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}=\frac{16 \sqrt{5}}{9}$. Then the desired radius of the circle with center $O$ is

$$
R=\frac{L N}{2 \sin \angle N M L}=\frac{16 \sqrt{5}}{9 \cdot 2 \cdot \frac{2}{3}}=\frac{4 \sqrt{5}}{3}
$$

question:
Booin D.A.

The whole family drank a full cup of coffee with milk, and Katya drank a quarter of all the milk and a sixth of all the coffee. How many people are in the family?

meta.gold_solution:
Let $n$ be the number of cups (the number of people in the family), and $x$ be the amount of milk consumed (in cups). Then the amount of coffee consumed is $n-x$. Katya drank one cup of coffee with milk, which consisted of one quarter of all the milk $(x / 4)$ and one sixth of all the coffee $((n-x) / 6)$. We get

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{x}{4}+\frac{(n-x)}{6}=1 \\
3 x+2(n-x)=12 \\
x+2 n=12
\end{gathered}
$$

Since $n$ is an integer, it follows from the last equation that $x$ is an integer, and even ($x=12 - 2 n$). Moreover, $x \leq n$, since the amount of milk consumed is certainly no more than the total amount of the drink.

By a small enumeration, we find that the last equation has three solutions:

$$
n=6, x=0 ; \quad n=5, x=2 ; \quad n=4, x=4 .
$$

The first and last solutions correspond to the case where everyone drank just milk or just coffee, while the second solution corresponds to the case where they drank coffee with milk.

## Answer

5 people.

question:
4. In a quiz, you answer 10 questions. Each question is either difficult or easy. For a difficult question, you get 5 points if you answer it correctly and -1 point if you answer it incorrectly; for an easy question, you get 3 points if you answer it correctly and -1 point if you answer it incorrectly. Moreover, if you answer a question correctly, the next one is difficult; if you answer a question incorrectly, the next one is easy. You start with a difficult question.

How many different final scores are possible after 10 questions?

meta.gold_solution:
B4. 27 To simplify the problem, we look at a variant of the quiz. We give one extra point for each question: 6 points for a correct answer to a difficult question, 4 points for a correct answer to an easy question, and 0 points for an incorrect answer. Everyone thus gets exactly 10 extra points, so the number of possible final scores does not change. We now see that all scores are divisible by 2, and we divide by 2 to make the problem even simpler. A participant now gets 3, 2, or 0 points for each question. This also does not change the number of possible final scores.

The final score is a maximum of 30 points (if all questions are answered correctly) and a minimum of 0 points (if all questions are answered incorrectly). We will now show that the final scores 1, 25, 28, and 29 are not possible, and that all other scores from 0 to 30 are possible.

The final scores $0,3,6, \ldots, 30$ can be achieved by first answering $0,1,2,3, \ldots, 10$ questions correctly and then answering all questions incorrectly.

The final scores $2,5,8, \ldots, 26$ can be achieved by first answering $9,8,7,6, \ldots, 1$ questions incorrectly, then answering an easy question correctly, and subsequently answering all difficult questions correctly.

The final scores $4,7,10, \ldots, 22$ can be achieved by first answering $7,6,5, \ldots, 1$ questions incorrectly, then answering an easy question correctly, a difficult question incorrectly, another easy question correctly, and all difficult questions correctly thereafter.

If at least one question is answered correctly, you already have at least 2 points. For this reason, the final score of 1 is not possible. If at least one question is answered incorrectly, you have at most $9 \cdot 3=27$ points. For this reason, the final scores of 28 and 29 are not possible. If exactly one question is answered incorrectly, two things can happen: the incorrectly answered question is the last question and you have $9 \cdot 3=27$ points, or the incorrectly answered question is not the last question and you have $8 \cdot 3+2=26$ points. If at least two questions are answered incorrectly, you have at most $8 \cdot 3=24$ points. For this reason, the final score of 25 is also not possible.

We see that the possible final scores (in the new quiz format) are the numbers from 0 to 30, with the exception of 1, 25, 28, and 29. (In the original quiz format, the possible final scores are the even numbers from -10 to 50, with the exception of $-8,40,46$, and 48.) There are thus 27 possible final scores.

question: In $\triangle A B C$; $A B=A C, C D$ is the altitude, $D M \perp B C, D N \perp A C$, $M, N$ are the feet of the perpendiculars. When $C D=D M+D N$, find $\frac{A B}{B C}$ (do not use trigonometric functions).

\Rightarrow b(CD-DN) \\
=a \cdot DM . \\
\because CD=DM+DN, \\
\therefore CD-DN=DM .
\end{array}
$$

Thus $b=a$, i.e., $\frac{AB}{BC}=\frac{b}{a}=1$.
At this point, $\triangle ABC$ is an equilateral triangle.
(2) As shown in Figure 2, when
$\angle A$ is an obtuse angle, extend $BA$ to $F$, such that $AF=$ $AB$, it is easy to know that $\triangle BCF$ is a right triangle. Since $CD \perp$ $BF$, we have $\angle BCD=\angle F$.

Take $CE=$ $b$ on $BC$, and connect $DE$.
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\because CD=DM+DN, \\
\therefore \frac{1}{2} b \cdot CD=\frac{1}{2} b \cdot DM+\frac{1}{2} b \cdot DN,
\end{array}
$$

i.e., $S_{\triangle ABC}=S_{\triangle DFC}+S_{\triangle DAC}$.
But $S_{\triangle ABC}=S_{\triangle ACF}=S_{\triangle FDC}+S_{\triangle DAC}$,
thus $S_{\triangle DEC}=S_{\triangle ADC}$.
From the proven $\angle ECD=\angle BCD=\angle F$, we know
$$
EC \cdot CD=CF \cdot DF \text {. }
$$

In the right $\triangle BCF$,
$$
\begin{array}{l}
CF=\sqrt{4b^2-a^2}, \\

question: Let $b$ and $c$ be fixed real numbers and let the ten points $(j,y_j )$ for $j=1,2,\ldots,10$ lie on the parabola $y =x^2 +bx+c.$ For $j=1,2,\ldots, 9$ let $I_j$ be the intersection of the tangents to the given parabola at $(j, y_j )$ and $(j+1, y_{j+1}).$ Determine the poynomial function $y=g(x)$ of least degree whose graph passes through all nine points $I_j .$

meta.gold_solution:
Given the parabola \( y = x^2 + bx + c \) and the points \( P(j, y_j) \) and \( Q(j+1, y_{j+1}) \), where \( y_j = j^2 + bj + c \) and \( y_{j+1} = (j+1)^2 + b(j+1) + c \).

1. **Find the equations of the tangents at \( P \) and \( Q \):**

   The derivative of \( y = x^2 + bx + c \) is \( y' = 2x + b \). Therefore, the slope of the tangent at \( P(j, y_j) \) is \( 2j + b \), and the equation of the tangent line at \( P \) is:
   \[
   y - y_j = (2j + b)(x - j)
   \]
   Substituting \( y_j = j^2 + bj + c \):
   \[
   y - (j^2 + bj + c) = (2j + b)(x - j)
   \]
   Simplifying:
   \[
   y = (2j + b)x - (2j + b)j + j^2 + bj + c
   \]
   \[
   y = (2j + b)x - 2j^2 - bj + j^2 + bj + c
   \]
   \[
   y = (2j + b)x - j^2 + c
   \]

   Similarly, the slope of the tangent at \( Q(j+1, y_{j+1}) \) is \( 2(j+1) + b = 2j + 2 + b \), and the equation of the tangent line at \( Q \) is:
   \[
   y - y_{j+1} = (2j + 2 + b)(x - (j+1))
   \]
   Substituting \( y_{j+1} = (j+1)^2 + b(j+1) + c \):
   \[
   y - ((j+1)^2 + b(j+1) + c) = (2j + 2 + b)(x - (j+1))
   \]
   Simplifying:
   \[
   y = (2j + 2 + b)x - (2j + 2 + b)(j+1) + (j+1)^2 + b(j+1) + c
   \]
   \[
   y = (2j + 2 + b)x - (2j + 2 + b)(j+1) + j^2 + 2j + 1 + bj + b + c
   \]
   \[
   y = (2j + 2 + b)x - (2j^2 + 2j + 2j + 2 + bj + b + 2j + 2 + b) + j^2 + 2j + 1 + bj + b + c
   \]
   \[
   y = (2j + 2 + b)x - j^2 - 2j - 1 + c
   \]

2. **Find the intersection \( I_j \) of the tangents:**

   Set the equations of the tangents equal to each other to find the intersection point \( I_j \):
   \[
   (2j + b)x - j^2 + c = (2j + 2 + b)x - (j^2 + 2j + 1) + c
   \]
   Simplifying:
   \[
   (2j + b)x - j^2 + c = (2j + 2 + b)x - j^2 - 2j - 1 + c
   \]
   \[
   (2j + b)x = (2j + 2 + b)x - 2j - 1
   \]
   \[
   0 = 2x - 2j - 1
   \]
   \[
   2x = 2j + 1
   \]
   \[
   x = j + \frac{1}{2}
   \]

   Substitute \( x = j + \frac{1}{2} \) back into one of the tangent equations to find \( y \):
   \[
   y = (2j + b)\left(j + \frac{1}{2}\right) - j^2 + c
   \]
   \[
   y = (2j + b)j + (2j + b)\frac{1}{2} - j^2 + c
   \]
   \[
   y = 2j^2 + bj + j + \frac{b}{2} - j^2 + c
   \]
   \[
   y = j^2 + bj + j + \frac{b}{2} + c
   \]
   \[
   y = j^2 + bj + j + \frac{b}{2} + c
   \]

3. **Eliminate \( j \) to find the polynomial function \( y = g(x) \):**

   Since \( x = j + \frac{1}{2} \), we have \( j = x - \frac{1}{2} \). Substitute \( j = x - \frac{1}{2} \) into the expression for \( y \):
   \[
   y = (x - \frac{1}{2})^2 + b(x - \frac{1}{2}) + (x - \frac{1}{2}) + \frac{b}{2} + c
   \]
   \[
   y = (x^2 - x + \frac{1}{4}) + b(x - \frac{1}{2}) + x - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{b}{2} + c
   \]
   \[
   y = x^2 - x + \frac{1}{4} + bx - \frac{b}{2} + x - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{b}{2} + c
   \]
   \[
   y = x^2 + bx + c - \frac{1}{4}
   \]

Thus, the polynomial function \( y = g(x) \) of least degree whose graph passes through all nine points \( I_j \) is:
\[
y = x^2 + bx + c - \frac{1}{4}
\]

The final answer is \( \boxed{ y = x^2 + bx + c - \frac{1}{4} } \).

question: Example 10 Find the smallest positive integer $n$, such that in any two-coloring of the complete graph $K_{n}$ with $n$ vertices, there always exist $m$ monochromatic edges, no two of which share a common endpoint.

meta.gold_solution:
Solution: It is clear that when $m=1$, $n=2$; when $m=2$, $n=5$. In fact, in the 2-colored $K_{4}$ as shown in Figure 7-11, any two segments of the same color have a common endpoint (solid lines represent red, dashed lines represent blue). However, in a 2-colored $K_{5}$, if all segments are the same color, there are certainly two segments of the same color without a common endpoint. Otherwise, there must be a red segment and a blue segment with a common endpoint. Let's assume $A_{1} A_{2}$ is red and $A_{2} A_{3}$ is blue. Clearly, regardless of the color of $A_{4} A_{5}$, there will be two segments of the same color without a common endpoint. This proves that when $m=2$, the smallest positive integer $n=5$.

Next, we use induction to prove that for all positive integers $m$, $n=3m-1$.

The proposition has been proven for $m=1,2$. Assume the proposition holds for $m=r$. When $m=r+1$, if all edges of $K_{3r+2}$ are the same color, there are certainly $r+1$ segments of the same color, none of which have a common endpoint; otherwise, there must be a vertex that is the common endpoint of a red edge and a blue edge. Removing the 3 endpoints of these two edges leaves $3r-1$ vertices. By the induction hypothesis, in the $K_{3r-1}$ with these $3r-1$ vertices, there exist $r$ segments of the same color, none of which have a common endpoint. Adding one of the two original segments of the same color, we obtain $r+1$ segments of the same color, none of which have a common endpoint.

On the other hand, divide the vertices of $K_{3r+1}$ into two groups: Group $A$ has $r$ vertices, and Group $B$ has $2r+1$ vertices. Color the segments between the vertices of Group $B$ red, and all other segments blue. Thus, whether the $r+1$ segments are red or blue, there will always be two segments with a common endpoint, indicating that the smallest positive integer $n=3r+2$. Therefore, we have completed the induction proof.

question: consider a $2008 \times 2008$ chess board. let $M$ be the smallest no of rectangles that can be drawn on the chess board so that sides of every cell of the board is contained in the sides of one of the rectangles. find the value of $M$. (eg for $2\times 3$ chessboard, the value of $M$ is 3.)

meta.gold_solution:
1. **Initial Setup and Strategy**:
   - We need to cover a $2008 \times 2008$ chessboard with the smallest number of rectangles such that every cell is contained within at least one rectangle.
   - We start by drawing the perimeter of the chessboard as one rectangle.
   - Then, we fill in the remaining cells by covering two rows or columns at a time.

2. **Optimality Argument**:
   - Suppose we have $x$ rectangles that cover the chessboard.
   - Define a rectangle as **covering** a row if one of its horizontal sides is contained in that row. Similarly, define **covering** columns.
   - Each rectangle can cover at most 4 rows/columns (2 rows and 2 columns).

3. **Unique Rows/Columns**:
   - Let $y$ be the number of rows/columns that are covered only once by any rectangle. Call these rows/columns **unique**.
   - **Claim**: For each rectangle, at most two of the rows/columns it covers can be unique.
   - **Proof**: If a rectangle covers three unique rows/columns, it must be the perimeter of the chessboard, which is not possible for internal rows/columns to be unique. Hence, at most two unique rows/columns per rectangle.

4. **Bounding the Number of Rectangles**:
   - From the claim, there are at least $\frac{y}{2}$ rectangles for which a row/column is unique.
   - Each of these rectangles can cover rows/columns not on the perimeter, leading to the inequality:
     \[
     4(x - y) + 2y \ge 4 \cdot 2007 - y
     \]
   - Simplifying, we get:
     \[
     4x - 2y \ge 4 \cdot 2007 - y \implies 4x \ge 4 \cdot 2007 + y \implies x \ge 2007 + \frac{y}{4}
     \]

5. **Improving the Bound**:
   - If $x = 2007$, then $y = 0$, meaning no row/column is unique, which is not possible.
   - Therefore, $x \ge 2008$.
   - To eliminate the case $x = 2008$, we improve the bound on the RHS to $4 \cdot 2007 - y + 4$ because the perimeter must also be covered:
     \[
     4x - 4y + 2y \ge 4 \cdot 2008 - y \implies 4x \ge 4 \cdot 2008 + y \implies x \ge 2008 + \frac{y}{4}
     \]
   - Hence, $x = 2008$ implies $y = 0$, which is not possible.

6. **Conclusion**:
   - Therefore, the smallest number of rectangles $M$ that can cover the $2008 \times 2008$ chessboard is $2009$.

The final answer is $\boxed{2009}$.

Problem 5.3. The figure shows a plan of the road system of a certain city. In this city, there are 8 straight streets, and 11 intersections are named with Latin letters $A, B, C, \ldots, J, K$.

Three police officers need to be placed at some intersections so that at least one police officer is on each of the 8 streets. Which three intersections should the police officers be placed at? It is sufficient to provide at least one suitable arrangement.

All streets run along straight lines.

Horizontal streets: $A-B-C-D, E-F-G, H-I-J-K$.

Vertical streets: $A-E-H, B-F-I, D-G-J$.

Diagonal streets: $H-F-C, C-G-K$.

meta.gold_solution:
Answer: $B, G, H$.

Solution. The option will work if police officers are placed at intersections $B, G, H$. It can be shown that this is the only possible option.

Since there are only three vertical streets, and each must have one police officer, there are definitely no police officers at intersections $C$ and $K$. Therefore, there must be a police officer at intersection $G$. Then, on street $E-F-G$, there are no more police officers (since there is at least one police officer on streets $A-B-C-D$ and $H-I-J-K$). On street $C-F-H$, there must be a police officer, and he can only be placed at intersection $H$. question:
Which is the quadratic equation whose roots are the squares of the roots of

$$
\sin 2 \alpha \cdot x^{2}-2(\sin \alpha+\cos \alpha) x+2=0
$$

Solve the thus obtained equation.

meta.gold_solution:
The roots of the given equation are:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_{1}=\frac{2(\sin \alpha+\cos \alpha)+2(\sin \alpha-\cos \alpha)}{4 \sin \alpha \cos \alpha}=\frac{1}{\sin \alpha} \\
& x_{2}=\frac{2(\sin \alpha+\cos \alpha)-2(\sin \alpha-\cos \alpha)}{4 \sin \alpha \cos \alpha}=\frac{1}{\sin \alpha}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the roots of the sought quadratic equation are:

$$
z_{1}=\frac{1}{\cos ^{2} \alpha}, z_{2}=\frac{1}{\sin ^{2} \alpha}
$$

So the equation is

$$
\sin ^{2} \alpha \cos ^{2} \alpha \cdot z^{2}-z+1=0
$$

or

$$
\sin ^{2} 2 \alpha \cdot z^{2}-4 z+4=0
$$

from which

$$
z=\frac{2(1 \pm \cos 2 \alpha)}{\sin ^{2} 2 \alpha}
$$

and thus

$$
z_{1}=\frac{1}{\sin ^{2} \alpha}, z_{2}=\frac{1}{\cos ^{2} \alpha}
$$

(Dénes Aladár, Györ.)

The problem was also solved by: Barna D., Friedmann B., Goldziher K., and Kármán T., Manheim E., Orlowszky F., Posgay B., Schiffer H., Szabó K., Weisz J.

9. (12 points) Three people, A, B, and C, depart from location $A$ to location $B$. A departs at 8:00, B at 8:20, and C at 8:30. They all travel at the same speed. 10 minutes after C departs, the distance from A to $B$ is exactly half the distance from B to $B$. At this moment, C is 2015 meters away from $B$. What is the distance between $A$ and $B$ in meters? $\qquad$

meta.gold_solution:
【Solution】Solution: According to the problem, we have:
Let the distance between Yi and Bing, which is 10 minutes of travel, be 1 unit;
The distance between Yi and Jia, which is 20 minutes of travel, is 2 units;
The distance from Jia to $B$ is equal to the distance between Jia and Yi, which is also 2 units.
Therefore, the distance from Bing to $B$ is 5 units corresponding to 2015, so 1 unit is $2015 \div 5=403$ meters.
The distance between Yi and Bing is also the distance Bing travels in 10 minutes, which is 1 unit, so the total distance is 6 units, which is: $403 \times 6=2418$ meters.

Therefore, the answer is: 2418.

question: Question: A student participates in military training and engages in target shooting, which must be done 10 times. In the 6th, 7th, 8th, and 9th shots, he scored 9.0 points, 8.4 points, 8.1 points, and 9.3 points, respectively. The average score of his first 9 shots is higher than the average score of his first 5 shots. If he wants the average score of 10 shots to exceed 8.8 points, how many points does he need to score at least in the 10th shot? (The points scored in each shot are accurate to 0.1 points)

meta.gold_solution:
Solution: From the given, the average score of the first 5 shots is less than
$$
\frac{9.0+8.4+8.1+9.3}{4}=8.7 \text{. }
$$

The total score of the first 9 shots is at most
$$
8.7 \times 9-0.1=78.2 \text{. }
$$

Therefore, the score of the tenth shot must be at least
$$
8.8 \times 10+0.1-78.2=9.9 \text{ (points). }
$$

The above solution, if we set the total score of the first 5 shots as $x$, and the score of the tenth shot as $y$, can be represented by the system of inequalities as
$$
\left.\begin{array}{l}
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\frac{x}{5}<8.7 \\
x<43.5
\end{array}\right. \\
\Rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x<53.2
\end{array} \text{ and the scores are accurate to } 0.1 \text{ points }
\end{array}\right\}
$$

Starting point: Assuming this student scores 9.9 points on the tenth shot, can his average score over 10 shots definitely exceed 8.8 points? The answer is not certain. For example, if the total score of the first 5 shots is 40 points (satisfying the given condition), then the total score of 10 shots is
$$
40+(9.0+8.4+8.1+9.3)+9.9=84.7<88
$$

The system of inequalities
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x<A \\
x+y<B

Problem 4. A set of at least three positive integers is called uniform if removing any of its elements the remaining set can be disjoint into two subsets with equal sums of elements. Find the minimal cardinality of a uniform set.

question:
15. Given the sequence $\left\{a_{n}\right\}(n \geqslant 0)$ satisfies $a_{0}=0$, for all non-negative integers $n$, we have
$$
a_{n+1}=2 \sqrt{30 a_{n}\left(a_{n}+1\right)}+11 a_{n}+5 .
$$

Find the general term formula for $a_{n}$.

meta.gold_solution:
15. $a_{n+1}=2 \sqrt{30 a_{n}\left(a_{n}+1\right)}+11 a_{n}+5>a_{n}$.

Subtract $11 a_{n} + 5$ from both sides of $a_{n+1}-11 a_{n}-5=2 \sqrt{30 a_{n}\left(a_{n}+1\right)}$ and square both sides, then rearrange to get
$$
\begin{array}{l}
a_{n}^{2}+a_{n+1}^{2}-22 a_{n} a_{n+1}-10 a_{n}-10 a_{n+1}+25=0 . \\
\text { Also, } a_{n-1}^{2}+a_{n}^{2}-22 a_{n-1} a_{n}-10 a_{n-1}-10 a_{n}+25=0,
\end{array}
$$

Subtract the two equations to get
$$
\begin{array}{l}
a_{n+1}^{2}-a_{n-1}^{2}-22 a_{n}\left(a_{n+1}-a_{n-1}\right)-10\left(a_{n+1}-a_{n-1}\right) \\
=0 .
\end{array}
$$

Since $a_{n+1}-a_{n-1}>0$, we have
$$
a_{n+1}+a_{n-1}-22 a_{n}-10=0 \text {. }
$$

Because $a_{n}+a_{n-2}-22 a_{n-1}-10=0$, subtract the two equations to get the homogeneous linear recurrence relation
$$
a_{n+1}-23 a_{n}+23 a_{n-1}-a_{n-2}=0 .
$$

The characteristic equation is $x^{3}-23 x^{2}+23 x-1=0$, with characteristic roots
$$
\lambda_{1}=1, \lambda_{2}=11+2 \sqrt{30}, \lambda_{3}=11-2 \sqrt{30} \text {. }
$$

Assume $a_{n}=C_{1}+C_{2}(11+2 \sqrt{30})^{n}+C_{3}(11-2 \sqrt{30})^{n}$.
Given $a_{0}=0, a_{1}=5, a_{2}=120$, we get
$$
C_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}, C_{2}=C_{3}=\frac{1}{4} \text {. }
$$

Therefore, the general term formula is
$$
a_{n}=-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}(11+2 \sqrt{30})^{n}+\frac{1}{4}(11-2 \sqrt{30})^{n} \text {. }
$$
(Provided by An Hai)

4. For a positive integer $n$ the number $P(n)$ is the product of the positive divisors of $n$. For example, $P(20)=8000$, as the positive divisors of 20 are $1,2,4,5,10$ and 20 , whose product is $1 \cdot 2 \cdot 4 \cdot 5 \cdot 10 \cdot 20=8000$.

meta.gold_solution:
4. a) Because $P(n)=15 n$ is the product of the positive divisors of $n$, the prime divisors 3 and 5 of $P(n)$ must also be divisors of $n$. It follows that $n$ is a multiple of 15 . If $n>15$, then 3, 5, 15 and $n$ are distinct divisors of $n$, yielding $P(n) \geqslant 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 15 \cdot n=225 n$. This contradicts the fact that $P(n)=15 n$. The only remaining possibility is $n=15$. This is indeed a solution, because $P(15)=1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 15=15 \cdot 15$.

b) Suppose that $P(n)=15 n^{2}$ holds. Again, we find that $n$ is a multiple of 15 . It is clear that $n=15$ is not a sulution, hence $n \geqslant 30$. We observe that $\frac{n}{5}>5$. It follows that $115$ holds, we have $P(n) \geqslant n \cdot n^{2}>15 n^{2}$, which contradicts the assumption of this problem. We conclude that no $n$ exists for which $P(n)=15 n^{2}$.

question: Mikulás is examining the sky. The next day, on his name day, he wants to travel as far as possible to bring gifts to the children. At midnight, it finally starts to snow. If the sleigh starts at the $S$ time point (at $(16-x$ hours) and, taking advantage of the maximum 8 hours of travel time, arrives at the $T$ time point (at $24-x$ hours), then the distance traveled by the sleigh is exactly the area of the pentagon $A S T B C$, which is the sum of the areas of the (possibly degenerate) trapezoids $A S M C$ and $C M T B$. According to the theorem of parallel chords,

$$
A S: C M=(16-x): 16
$$

thus

$$
A S=m\left(1-\frac{x}{16}\right)
$$

Similarly, $B T: C M=x: 8$, so

$$
B T=\frac{m x}{8}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
t_{A S M C}+t_{C M T B} & =\frac{x}{2} m\left(2-\frac{x}{16}\right)+\frac{8-x}{2} m\left(1+\frac{x}{8}\right)= \\
& =\frac{3 m}{32}\left(-\left(x-\frac{16}{3}\right)^{2}+\frac{256}{9}\right)+4 m
\end{aligned}
$$

it is the largest when $x=\frac{16}{3}$; therefore, Mikulás sets off at 10:40 AM.

\left(d_{1} d_{2} d_{3}\right)^{2} \mid p_{1} p_{2} p_{3} d_{1} d_{2} d_{3}, \quad \text { or } \quad d_{1} d_{2} d_{3} \mid p_{1} p_{2} p_{3}
$$

On the other hand, by multiplying the three inequalities $p_{i} \leq d_{i}$, we obtain $p_{1} p_{2} p_{3} \leq d_{1} d_{2} d_{3}$. From the conclusions of the last two sentences, it follows that $d_{1} d_{2} d_{3} = p_{1} p_{2} p_{3}$ must hold. From the way the inequality $p_{1} p_{2} p_{3} \leq d_{1} d_{2} d_{3}$ was derived, we see that $d_{i} = p_{i}$ or $n_{i} = p_{i}^{2}$ must hold for each $i=1,2,3$. Since the number of decompositions is finite, the maximum value must exist, so we can assume the decomposition $\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{10}\right)$, where $x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{10}=1989$, is one of the decompositions with the largest product $x_{1} x_{2} \cdots x_{10}$. If any of $x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{10}$ is less than 198, let it be $x_{1}$, then there must be one greater than 198, let it be $x_{10}$. Let $x_{1}^{\prime}=x_{1}+\left(x_{10}-198\right), x_{10}^{\prime}=198$, then we get a new decomposition $\left(x_{1}^{\prime}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{9}, x_{10}^{\prime}\right)$, with the corresponding product $x^{\prime}{ }_{1} x_{2} \cdots x_{9} x_{10}^{\prime}$. Therefore, $x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{10}$ are all not less than 198. If any of $x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{10}$ is greater than 199, let it be $x_{1}$, then there must be one less than 199, let it be $x_{10}$. Since $x_{10}$ is not less than 198, so $x_{10}=$ 198. But $x_{1}^{\prime} x_{10}^{\prime}-x_{1} x_{10}=\left(x_{1}-1\right)\left(x_{10}+1\right)-$ $x_{1} x_{10}=x_{1} x_{10}+x_{1}-x_{10}-1-x_{1} x_{10}=x_{1}-x_{10}-1=x_{1}-198-1=x_{1}-$ $199>0$, so $x_{1}^{\prime} x_{2} \cdots x_{9} x_{10}^{\prime}>x_{1} x_{2} \cdots x_{10}$, which is a contradiction. Therefore, $x_{1}, x_{2}, \cdots, x_{10}$ can only be 199 or 198, thus the decomposition: $199+199+\cdots+199+198$ corresponds to the product $199^{9} \times 198$ being the largest.

$$
f(n)-f(n-1)=\frac{n^{2}}{2006}-\frac{(n-1)^{2}}{2006}=\frac{2 n-1}{2006}1003$,
$$
f(n)-f(n-1)=\frac{2 n-1}{2006}>1
$$

Moreover, since
$$
f(1004)=\frac{1004^{2}}{2006}=\frac{(1003+1)^{2}}{2006}=\frac{1003^{2}}{2006}+\frac{2 \times 1003}{2006}+\frac{1}{2006}=501.5+1+\frac{1}{2006}>502,

question: Three friends, Xenia, Yvett, and Zita, each arrive at an internet café that is open from noon to 8 PM, at independently and randomly chosen times, each staying for one hour. What is the probability that all three of them meet?

meta.gold_solution:
I. solution. Let's assume that Xénia, Yvett, and Zita arrive at the internet café $x, y$, and $z$ hours after 12 o'clock. Since each of them stays exactly one hour and the café is open until 8 PM, they all need to arrive by 7 PM, i.e., $0 \leq x \leq 7, 0 \leq y \leq 7$, and $0 \leq z \leq 7$. We can represent the arrival times of the three girls as ordered triples of points $P(x; y; z)$ in space, and the measure of the event space as the volume of the set of points. In this case, the entire event space is a cube with an edge length of 7 units, whose volume is 343 cubic units.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_02_2e51b95f23022e6ad5d2g-1.jpg?height=545&width=616&top_left_y=394&top_left_x=749)

The conditions for the girls to meet are:

$$
|x-y| \leq 1 \Longleftrightarrow x-1 \leq y \leq x+1, \quad|y-z| \leq 1 \Longleftrightarrow y-1 \leq z \leq y+1
$$

and

$$
|z-x| \leq 1 \Longleftrightarrow z-1 \leq x \leq z+1
$$

The condition for the three girls to meet is that the point $P(x; y; z)$ representing their arrival times is located within the cube with an edge length of 7 units, between the planes $y=x-1$ and $y=x+1$, $z=y-1$ and $z=y+1$, and $x=z-1$ and $x=z+1$. This region represents the favorable cases and can be divided into a cube with a side length of 1 unit and 3 oblique prisms with a square base, each with a height of 6 units. The diagram shows one such square-based oblique prism (prism ABCDLMNK).

Thus, the volume of the region is $1 + 3 \cdot 6 = 19$ cubic units. The desired probability is: $p = \frac{19}{343}$.

II. solution. Divide one hour into $n$ small time units. Since the girls each stay for one hour at the internet café, they cannot arrive in the last hour, leaving 7 hours, or $7n$ time units. From these, we select one for each girl to enter the café. The total number of cases can be easily counted: independently, each can choose any of the $7n$ time points, so this is $(7n)^3 = 343n^3$ cases.

The favorable cases are when all three arrive within the same hour. Since the café opens at noon, if the last to arrive does so within the first hour, they will definitely meet, which is $n^3$ cases, as each of the three can choose any of the first $n$ time points.

For the other cases, consider when the last to arrive arrives: this can be in $6n$ different ways. If this last person arrives alone, the other two can choose from the previous $n-1$ time points, and it matters who was the last, which can happen in 3 ways, so this is $3(n-1)^2$ cases. If two arrive last at the same time, the third can arrive in $(n-1)$ time points, and again, it must be multiplied by 3 because the two who arrived last can be any of the three, which is $3(n-1)$ cases. When all three arrive in the same time unit, this is one case. The sum of these must be multiplied by $6n$, because the arrival time of the last person can be any of $6n$.

This is a total of

$$
6n\left(3(n-1)^2 + 3(n-1) + 1\right) = 18n^3 - 18n^2 + 6n
$$

cases.

The probability that all three meet is the number of favorable cases divided by the total number of cases:

$$
\frac{n^3 + 18n^3 - 18n^2 + 6n}{343n^3} = \frac{19n^3 - 18n^2 + 6n}{343n^3} = \frac{19}{343} - \frac{18}{343n} + \frac{6}{343n^2}
$$

We need to examine what this expression approaches as $n$ approaches infinity, since in reality there are infinitely many time points in the 7 hours when they can arrive. Since the last two terms approach zero, the entire expression approaches $\frac{19}{343}$, so this is the probability that all three will meet.

question: 5. A square is paved with regular hexagonal tiles with a side length of $36 \mathrm{~cm}$. Now, a circular disc with a radius of $6 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{~cm}$ is tossed upwards. The probability that the disc, upon landing, does not intersect with the gaps between the tiles is approximately $\qquad$

meta.gold_solution:
5. $\frac{4}{9}$.

To ensure the circular disc does not overlap the gaps between the tiles, the center of the disc must fall within a smaller regular hexagon that is centered with the tile and has sides parallel to the tile edges, with a distance of $6 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{~cm}$ (as shown in Figure 5). Construct $O C_{1} \perp A_{1} A_{2}$, and $C_{1} C_{2}=6 \sqrt{3} \mathrm{~cm}$.
Since $A_{1} A_{2}=A_{2} O=36, A_{2} C_{1}=18$, therefore, $C_{1} O=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} A_{2} O=18 \sqrt{3}$.
Then $C_{2} O=C_{1} O-C_{1} C_{2}=12 \sqrt{3}$.
Also, since $C_{2} O=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} B_{2} O$, therefore,
$$
B_{2} O=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} C_{2} O=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \times 12 \sqrt{3}=24 \text {. }
$$

And $B_{1} B_{2}=B_{2} O$, so the side length of the smaller regular hexagon is $24 \mathrm{~cm}$. Therefore, the required probability is
$$
P=\frac{\text { area of the smaller regular hexagon }}{\text { area of the regular hexagon tile }}=\frac{B_{1} B_{2}^{2}}{A_{1} A_{2}^{2}}=\frac{24^{2}}{36^{2}}=\frac{4}{9} \text {. }
$$

The integers from $1$ to $n$ are written, one on each of $n$ cards. The first player removes one card. Then the second player removes two cards with consecutive integers. After that the first player removes three cards with consecutive integers. Finally, the second player removes four cards with consecutive integers.
What is th smallest value of $n$ for which the second player can ensure that he competes both his moves?

meta.gold_solution:
1. **Show that \( n = 13 \) does not work:**

   - Suppose the first player removes the card with number \( 4 \).
   - The second player has the option to remove two consecutive cards. Consider the following scenarios:
     - If the second player removes the pair \( (8, 9) \) or \( (9, 10) \):
       - If the second player removes \( (8, 9) \), the first player can then remove \( (10, 11, 12) \).
       - If the second player removes \( (9, 10) \), the first player can then remove \( (5, 6, 7) \).
       - In both cases, the second player cannot find four consecutive numbers to remove in their next move.
     - If the second player does not remove \( (8, 9) \) or \( (9, 10) \):
       - The first player can then remove \( (8, 9, 10) \).
       - The remaining cards are \( (1, 2, 3), (5, 6, 7), (11, 12, 13) \), and the second player cannot find four consecutive numbers to remove in their next move.

2. **Show that \( n = 14 \) works:**

   - Let the first player remove the card with number \( k \).
   - We have two groups of consecutive numbers: \( k-1 \) numbers on one side and \( 14-k \) numbers on the other side.
   - Without loss of generality, assume \( k-1 \leq 14-k \), which implies \( k \leq 7 \).
   - Consider the following cases:
     - If \( k-1 \geq 4 \):
       - The second player can remove the pair \( (k+1, k+2) \).
       - This leaves two groups: \( (1, 2, 3, \ldots, k) \) and \( (k+3, k+4, \ldots, 14) \), each with more than 4 elements.
       - The second player can always find four consecutive numbers to remove in their next move.
     - If \( k = 4 \) or \( k = 3 \):
       - The second player can remove the pair \( (1, 2) \).
       - This leaves at least 10 consecutive numbers, and no matter how the first player removes 3 consecutive numbers, there will still be 4 consecutive numbers left for the second player to remove.
     - If \( k = 1 \) or \( k = 2 \):
       - The second player can remove the pair \( (3, 4) \).
       - This leaves at least 10 consecutive numbers, and no matter how the first player removes 3 consecutive numbers, there will still be 4 consecutive numbers left for the second player to remove.

Therefore, the smallest value of \( n \) for which the second player can ensure that he completes both his moves is \( n = 14 \).

The final answer is \( \boxed{14} \).

question: 4. A magician and his assistant have a deck of cards, all of which have the same back, and the front is one of 2017 colors (each color has 1000000 cards). The magic trick is: the magician first leaves the room, the audience arranges $n$ face-up cards in a row on the table, the magician's assistant then flips $n-1$ of these cards over in their original positions, leaving only one card face-up, and then the magician enters the room, observes the cards on the table, and selects a face-down card, guessing its color. Find the minimum value of $n$, such that the magician and his assistant can complete this trick according to a predetermined strategy.

meta.gold_solution:
4. When $n=2018$, the magician and the assistant can agree that for $i=1,2, \cdots, 2017$, if the assistant keeps the $i$-th card face up, the magician will guess that the 2018-th card is of the $i$-th color. This way, the magic trick can be completed.

Assume for some positive integer $n \leqslant 2017$, the magic trick can be completed.

For convenience, use $(a, i)$ to denote that the $a$-th card is of the $i$-th color, where $1 \leqslant a \leqslant n, 1 \leqslant i \leqslant 2017$.

For $n$ cards, note that the number of cards of each color is 1000000 (greater than $n$), so there are $2017^{n}$ different states (each position has 2017 possible colors). Each state is equivalent to a set of the form
$$
\left\{\left(1, i_{1}\right),\left(2, i_{2}\right), \cdots,\left(n, i_{n}\right)\right\}
$$
where $i_{1}, i_{2}, \cdots, i_{n} \in\{1,2, \cdots, 2017\}$.
For any $a, i$, since when the magician sees $(a, i)$, they can always guess at least one $(b, j)(b \neq a)$, and the number of states containing $(a, i)$ and $(b, j)$ is only $2017^{n-2}$, the total number of different states the magician can guess (i.e., $2017^{n}$) does not exceed $2017 \times 2017^{n-2} n$.
Thus, $n \geqslant 2017$.
This indicates that $n$ can only be 2017. Therefore, from any $(a, i)$, the $(b, j)(b \neq a)$ that can be guessed is unique.

Therefore, draw an edge from $(a, i)$ to $(b, j)$, denoted as $(a, i) \rightarrow(b, j)$, and call $a, b$ "associated" (association is mutual, i.e., $b, a$ are also associated), and any two different guesses $(a, i) \rightarrow(b, j)$ and $(c, k) \rightarrow(d, l)$ cannot correspond to the same state.
This indicates that at least one of $c, d$ belongs to $\{a, b\}$.
The following lemma is proved.
Lemma If $(a, i) \rightarrow(b, j)$, then there must exist $k \neq i$ such that $(b, j) \rightarrow(a, k)$.

Proof Suppose $(b, j) \rightarrow(c, k)$. If $c \neq a$ or $(c, k)=(a, i)$, then a state containing $(a, i), (b, j), (c, k)$ has two guesses $(a, i) \rightarrow(b, j)$ and $(b, j) \rightarrow(c, k)$, which is a contradiction.
Thus, there must exist a $k \neq i$ such that
$(b, j) \rightarrow(a, k)$.
The lemma is proved.
Assume without loss of generality that 1 and 2 are associated.
Note that 3 must be associated with another number $a$. By the previous discussion, $a \in\{1,2\}$, assume without loss of generality that $a=1$.

At this point, for any $b(4 \leqslant b \leqslant 2017)$, since $b$ must be associated with another number $c$, and 1 and 2 are associated, 1 and 3 are associated, thus $c \in\{1,2\}, c \in\{1,3\}$. Therefore, $c=1$, i.e., 1 and $b$ are associated.
This indicates that 2, 3, ..., 2017 are all associated with 1.
Thus, for any $t \in\{2,3, \cdots, 2017\}$, combining the lemma, there exist $i_{t}, j_{t} \in\{1,2, \cdots, 2017\}$ such that $\left(1, i_{t}\right) \rightarrow\left(t, j_{t}\right)$.

Using the lemma repeatedly, there exist $k_{t}, l_{t} \in\{1,2, \cdots, 2017\}\left(k_{t} \neq i_{t}, l_{t} \neq j_{t}\right)$ such that
$\left(t, j_{t}\right) \rightarrow\left(1, k_{t}\right) \rightarrow\left(t, l_{t}\right)$.
Thus, $i_{2}, k_{2}, i_{3}, k_{3}, \cdots, i_{2017}, k_{2017}$ are all different, but $2 \times 2016 > 2017$, which is a contradiction. This indicates that the case $n=2017$ cannot complete the magic trick.
In summary, the minimum value of $n$ is 2018.

Also, $\triangle G D O$, $\triangle O I F$, and $\triangle H O E$ are all similar to $\triangle A B C$. Since the ratio of the areas of similar triangles is equal to the square of the similarity ratio, we have:
$$
\begin{array}{l}
